description: We are Team mazennn, working on the "Abandoned but not Forgotten" challenge. We're building an interactive storytelling website that introduces school-age space fans to the hardware NASA left on the Moon and Mars, and the science it made possible. We enjoy web development, design and storytelling. We welcome teammates with skills in coding, graphic design, writing or space science!
summary: Left Behind is an interactive storytelling website that introduces school-age space fans to the hardware NASA has left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. Students explore clickable maps, open the story of each machine (from Apollo's laser mirrors to the Ingenuity helicopter and the Voyager probes), see whether it still works, and learn the science it made possible. A timeline and a quiz help them remember what they learned. We built it because these machines are part of our history and many still teach us today, but most students have never heard their stories.
details:
What it does: Left Behind is an interactive website that tells the stories of 20 pieces of NASA hardware left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space, for school-age space fans. Users pick a world, tap a location on a clickable map, and open a story card. Each card explains what the hardware was, where it is now, whether it still works (Active, Retired or Gone), a "Did you know?" fact, and the science it made possible.

Features: maps of the Moon's near side and of Mars that show the real landing locations, a deep-space view of the Voyager, Pioneer, New Horizons and Cassini missions, a 1969–2025 timeline, a "Why it matters" section, and a 5-question quiz with explanations.

Benefits: it turns "space junk" into history and science that young learners can explore. It shows that many of these machines still matter today. For example, scientists still bounce lasers off the Apollo mirrors and still receive data from the Voyagers.

How we built it: HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single page, with an animated starfield and SVG maps, hosted on Vercel. It works on phones and computers.

Goal: to make students curious about space exploration and to help them understand how each mission built on the ones before it.
